title: Data Scientist but I want to do AI Game Dev as a hobby
author: combrade
selftext:
I'm a data scientist, and I work about 55 hours per week. I really want to create telltale or narrative story games based off of books that I've read that I know will never get adapted to a video game or even just a movie. I wouldn’t sell it probably just distribute to a few of my friends . 

The main languages I just know and work with are Python SQL and R.  I don’t know any C# . I’m familiar with agentic coding but not familiar with say the Unity editor . I have played around with Astra and Blender.

Given my limited time, what can I learn so I can just go into game development right away but still kind of know what I'm doing? I'm not a huge fan of the label  of vibe coding. I like to say, especially at my work, that we do agentic coding. We should try to understand either the code or system design behind what we're building. 

What can I learn that would really give me the bang for my buck, so I know what the hell I'm doing? Should it just be the Unity Editor and a bit of C#? Also , should I just pick up some type of Unity AI editor or plugin like Bezi?

comments.author: BanjoThunderbird
comments.body:
Honestly just iron out exactly what you want your game to look like, write up some design docs and then talk to Astra about what the best engine for your project would be. Unreal, Godot and Unity are all super solid and have different optimal use cases but you're best off not overthinking. Just dive into one and learn some skills because it's quite transferable and probably doesn't matter too much.   
  
As someone who was in a similar position (software engineer who got into gamedev while not having a lot of time), 55hr a week is fkn heavy and you probably don't have the time to do much more than what I'd describe as vibe coding unless you're a dead-set genius with godlike executive function. What I've found is that game development is a skill about attention to detail, and you'll very quickly hit the point where all of your time is spent making a million tiny improvements that individual won't be noticed but together make a great game.

replies.author: combrade
replies.body: Should I consider those  Humble Bundle for Video Game Assets ? They often sell either just game assets , audio or character voices which seem useful.

replies.author: BanjoThunderbird
replies.body: Does it look like it has stuff that's thematically cohesive for the game you want to make?

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
I mean, if you're going for simple, and narrative, then you can go with Ren'Py and a lot of the technical stuff is handheld for you. Your main concern is navigating the story, ideally while presenting choices, and posting all the renders and setting up cutscenes. Renders are easy enough, if time consuming. Cutscenes are a lot harder, technically, but you could have AI produce video based on your renders to get virtually the same results but without it taking days of time for a  45 second cut.

You don't really need to know Unity or Godot to work in it with agents. Unreal you have to understand more, currently, but once v6 hits I suspect UE is going to be the  most AI friendly engine for traditional games. You CAN set up scenes for a narrative game in Unity/Unreal/Godot/etc. But you'll have to do a lot more of systems implementation for a narrative game because these engines are not designed for it out of the box. They're designed to accommodate all kinds of games, and a lot of the development goes into improving performance for things like physics, world generation, etc... Most of which becomes irrelevant and extraneous in a game that's largely about telling a story and not about the gameplay.
